text: We still bill hourly and every month there is an invoice dispute with at least one client. I keep wondering whether fixed-scope pricing would just move the arguments to the start of the project.

Our support inbox first reply time is around 8 hours and the reviews are getting worse. I think the fix is more features, but my cofounder says the fix is replying faster. Who is right here, from your experience?
Hot take: everyone obsessing over evals is wasting time. When our model regressed we switched to a bigger model and it fixed most of it. Eval sets are overrated for small client builds.
Every automation project we sold as automate everything turned into a mess of edge cases. I'm starting to think we should only scope one inbox or one workflow per project at the start.
We spent three months reading analytics dashboards to plan the roadmap. Last week I did a handful of customer calls and learned more in five days than in the whole quarter.
I keep rejecting people with messy CVs and I suspect I'm missing good builders. Has anyone replaced CV screening with a short paid trial project, and did the hires actually turn out better?
Our daily standup is 30 minutes for a team of six and half of it is people waiting their turn. I'm thinking of moving it to written updates but worry we lose the team feeling.
Looked at our churn data this week and the pattern is clear: clients who never finish onboarding in the first two weeks leave within three months. Onboarding is the real retention lever.
I do my best work after midnight and I think the advice to stop working late is overrated for founders. My output dropped every time I tried to keep normal hours.
Coaching my kid's football team this season taught me that the captain who passes the ball is worth more than the one who scores. I'm now trying to delegate the same way at work.
Every proposal I send has one price and every client tries to haggle it down. Thinking of trying tiered options in our proposals so clients compare tiers instead of arguing about the number.
We built a client automation that only our team can turn off, and now every small change is a support ticket for us. Next time the client's own staff need a switch they control.
Should I keep my day job or go full time on my studio? Deciding this week. A part-time contract would cover rent, and I'm torn between that safety and the freedom to say no to bad-fit clients.
Right now I'm deciding between raising my price or offering three tiers in my proposals. I'm stuck and overthinking it, and clients keep haggling over the one price I quote.
We just shipped our product: a scheduling tool for Riverside Dental Clinics. Our startup is three people, we launched it to 14 clinics and ten customer calls in one week changed our roadmap.
Hiring is hard this year. Not sure what to do about it yet, maybe try something new soon.
I built an onboarding checklist tool after we noticed churn came from clients who never finished onboarding. There is a waitlist if that sounds useful to your team.
Keeping a part-time contract while starting my studio feels like cheating, but it means I can say no to clients who are a bad fit for us.
Thinking about evals for our small LLM project. How many examples do people use before it is worth it?
Tried a no screens after 10pm rule for two weeks. Slept better, not sure about output yet.
